summary: Built the four authored Apex classes and the verbatim TestDataFactory copy for M3-S03: OpportunityApprovalService (the body, one SOQL with WITH USER_MODE and one Approval.process(requests, false)), OpportunityApprovalController (@AuraEnabled, what the M3-S04 LWC imports), OpportunityApprovalSubmitAction (the single @InvocableMethod, List-in/List-out, one result per input in input order) and OpportunityApprovalServiceTest (six methods covering all three classes and three refusal paths, persona runAs per test-class-standards gotcha 13, system-mode fixture seed per gotcha 15). Ten of ten declared outputs written; check-outputs ok; all three declared checker tests exit 0 and each was proven live against a deliberately broken scratch copy. Two of those probes failed on first attempt and exposed real defects that are now fixed or written up: a named constant hid the approval-process name from check_approval_process_apex_patterns.py so its resolution rule was silently inert, and check_test_class_standards.py reads comments as code on its runAs path in both directions (a prose runAs call satisfied the ERROR; 97 possessive apostrophes in comments then blanked all seven real runAs calls). The run instruction to stamp 67.0 was refused in favour of the plan's 62.0. No compile check was possible and nothing was deployed.
confidence_rationale: AGENT_CONTRACT.md Gate C row 3 caps confidence at MEDIUM when no offline compile check ran, and none could: there is no offline Apex compiler in the sf CLI and no org alias was supplied. Everything else meets the HIGH bar — all mandatory inputs came from plan.json, every recommendation cites a skill or template that exists, every emitted identifier resolves to a template file or a cited skill line, and all three declared checkers exit 0 with their liveness proven. Two inline UNVERIFIED markers (the Percent reading under A35, the Sales User profile name) are declared-assumption readings rather than unresolved symbols, so GATES.md Gate B's one-unresolved-symbol LOW rule does not apply.

dimensions_skipped.reason: ApplicationLogger is deliberately not wired: the step declares include_logger false, and the plan note records why — SecurityUtils references ApplicationLogger, which references Application_Log__c (eight fields) and Logger_Setting__mdt (one), a closure no step in this plan ships. Failures are therefore carried back to the caller as a SubmitOutcome message (Q30) rather than logged anywhere, which is what Q30 asked for but is not observability.

Coverage is an estimate, not a measurement: no test run was possible without an org, and scripts/mock_deploy.py --test-level is the human's to run. The catch (DmlException) block in submitBatch is named as the branch expected to stay uncovered.

findings.title: A declared acceptance test was exiting 0 having checked nothing, because a named constant hid the process name from the checker
findings.detail: check_approval_process_apex_patterns.py's RE_PROCESS_NAME matches only a string literal inside setProcessDefinitionNameOrId(...). The first draft passed a private static final constant, so the checker found no process name in the Apex at all, skipped its resolution rule and exited 0. Liveness probe C — renaming the process to Discount_Approval_Typo — did not fire, which is how it surfaced. The plan's own step note assumed the opposite ('check_approval_process_apex_patterns.py resolved that string against Opportunity.Discount_Approval.approvalProcess-meta.xml in a fixture run').
findings.recommendation: Fixed in this step: the developer name is now written inline at the call with a comment saying why. Library follow-up: the checker could also resolve a name reached through a same-class String constant, so that better Apex does not silently withdraw the assertion.

findings.title: check_test_class_standards.py reads comments as code on its runAs path, producing both a false pass and a false fail on this step's own file
findings.detail: has_permissioned_runas, runas_arguments and find_fixture_seeded_as_persona all call strip_literals(text) on the raw file and never strip_comments, although the same module defines an offset-preserving strip_comments for exactly this purpose. False pass: the prose 'System.runAs(<permissioned rep>)' in a header comment satisfied the user-mode-test-without-runas ERROR on its own, and liveness probe B did not fire. False fail: with that prose removed, 97 possessive apostrophes in ordinary comments each opened a phantom string literal, and strip_literals blanked all seven real System.runAs calls — measured as 'raw runAs: 7 | after strip_literals: 0' — so the ERROR fired on a class that runs every assertion as a permissioned persona.
findings.recommendation: Worked around here, not fixed: the test class is written without possessive apostrophes in comments and without a spelled-out runAs call in prose, and both probes now behave. The real fix belongs in the library — strip comments before stripping literals on those three functions, with a comment-only and a real fixture, the same shape as the 2026-09-16 comment-aware sweep that did not reach this path. Same class of defect as apex/apex-security-patterns gotcha 'A Checker That Reads Comments As Code Flags Safe Classes'.

findings.title: apex/apex-security-patterns is cited in skills[] with no test running its checker, and declaring one today would block the step
findings.detail: build_plan.py next prints the standing advice. Run by hand, check_apex_security_patterns.py --manifest-dir artefacts/M3-S03 exits 1 with three findings, none fixable inside this step: two HIGH 'user-facing entry point lacks obvious read-access enforcement' against OpportunityApprovalController and OpportunityApprovalSubmitAction — a per-file heuristic meeting the deliberate three-class split of decision D6, where enforcement lives one call away in the service — and one MEDIUM 'public/global Apex class has no explicit sharing declaration (apiVersion 67.0)' against TestDataFactory.cls, the canonical template this step ships verbatim by contract. Widening scope to build does not help, because the rule never leaves the file.
findings.recommendation: Three real options for the human, in order of preference: (1) fix the template — give templates/apex/tests/TestDataFactory.cls an explicit sharing keyword, which clears the MEDIUM for every build that ships it; (2) teach the checker that a class whose only body is a delegation to another class in the same tree is not an unenforced entry point; (3) drop apex/apex-security-patterns from this step's skills[] if the answer is that its checker cannot express what this step needs. Declaring the checker unchanged would block M3-S03 on findings its own plan created.

findings.title: The run instruction to build at API 67.0 contradicts plan.json in three places; the plan was followed
findings.detail: The runner was told to stamp 67.0 as the earlier scenarios' Apex did. steps[M3-S03].inputs.api_version is '62.0'; the step note argues the 62.0/67.0 split at length and calls it deliberate; and manual acceptance test 6 pins it, ticking only if the four authored classes carry 62.0 while TestDataFactory carries 67.0. Under section 2 the plan is the only shared state, so 62.0 was used. This is not only a number: at 62.0 the default access mode is system mode and the explicit WITH USER_MODE on the service's one SOQL is what enforces FLS, whereas at 67.0 user mode is the default and the keyword states intent rather than providing the mechanism.
findings.recommendation: If 67.0 is genuinely wanted for the build's Apex, it is an amend-step on inputs.api_version AND on manual acceptance test 6, followed by a documented -> running re-run of this step — not a runner-side edit. Raising the build's API version has stayed a plan-level decision in M1-S02, M2-S05, M3-S01 and M3-S02 alike.

findings.title: OpportunityApprovalService exposes submitBatch, which the single-record requirement did not name
findings.detail: The feature summary says 'Submit exactly one', and by agents/apex-builder/AGENT.md Step 7 anything the approved requirement does not call for is a deviation to surface rather than a bonus. submitBatch exists because @InvocableMethod is a List-in / List-out contract and Flow hands the action a whole batch of interviews: looping submitOne would have put one SOQL and one Approval.process per input inside a loop. That defect would not have been caught by any declared checker — IM005 matches literal SOQL brackets and DML keywords, not a service call that performs them. submitOne remains the requirement's capability and the only method the controller calls.
findings.recommendation: Accept it, or have the plan verifier rule that the invocable surface should be dropped and the action rebuilt as controller-only. Do not resolve it by looping submitOne.
